plan: Complete enhanced-ACT paired-passage set (CLD-P-ACT-R-000034, 'Choosing by Default'): an economist's case for automatic enrollment and a policy writer's account of how the same inertia locks people in. 9 questions: 3 on Passage A, 3 on Passage B, 3 across both. Checked against the bank's only other paired social-science set (027, library fines) to avoid its argument shape (evidence-quality critique) and its question templates ('B regards A's case as', 'B would respond to A's report').

passages.title: Choosing by Default (paired passages)
passages.text:
SOCIAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an essay by an economist; Passage B is from an essay by a policy writer. Both are original texts written for this practice set.

Passage A

In the late 1990s, a large American company changed one rule in its benefits paperwork. New employees had previously been required to sign up if they wanted to join the company's retirement savings plan; now they were enrolled automatically unless they filled out a form to opt out. Nothing else about the plan changed. The company's matching contributions, the investment choices, and the employees' freedom to leave the plan were all exactly as before.

The effect was striking. Among workers hired under the old rule, fewer than half had joined the plan within their first year or so. Among workers hired under the new rule, participation was close to ninety percent. Economists who studied the change found that the difference was largest among the employees who were least likely to save on their own: younger workers and those with lower incomes.

Findings like this one have made the default a favorite tool of policymakers. A default does not forbid anything or cost anyone money; it simply decides what happens when a person does nothing. Because doing nothing is what most people do most of the time, the choice of a default is never neutral. Someone has to choose it, and choosing it well can accomplish what years of reminders and lectures about saving could not.

To its supporters, that is the appeal of the approach: it respects people's freedom while acknowledging that freedom is exercised by busy, distracted human beings.

Passage B

No one disputes that automatic enrollment gets people into retirement plans. What the early studies also revealed, though less loudly, is that it tends to keep people wherever it puts them. Most automatically enrolled workers stayed at the plan's default contribution rate, which was often low, and left their money in the default investment, which was often a cautious fund that grew slowly. Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less. The default pulled them in and then held them in place.

This is not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself, seen from the other side. A default works because people tend to stay with whatever requires no action. That same tendency means that a poorly chosen default is hard to escape, and that its effects can last for decades, quietly, in millions of accounts.

Some designers have tried to put that tendency to better use. In one well-known program, employees agreed in advance to have their contribution rate rise automatically each time they received a raise. Because the increases came out of future pay rather than the pay employees already had, few people objected, and few later bothered to stop them; within a few years, participants' average savings rate had more than tripled. The lesson is not that defaults are good or bad but that the default is the policy. Whoever sets it is deciding for everyone who never gets around to deciding.

candidates.stem: In Passage A, the author most likely includes the statement "Nothing else about the plan changed" in order to:

choices.A: rule out other explanations for the rise in participation that followed.
choices.B: suggest that the company's retirement plan was unusually generous.
choices.C: emphasize that employees were not told about the change in the rule.
choices.D: show that the company was reluctant to change its other policies.

candidates.evidence: Nothing else about the plan changed.
candidates.explanation: By stressing that only the enrollment rule changed, the author lets the jump in participation be attributed to the default rather than to better matching or new investments.

B.rationale: Nothing compares the plan with others; the sentence stresses that the plan stayed the same.

C.rationale: Employees could opt out by form, and nothing says the change was hidden.

D.rationale: The sentence isolates one change; it says nothing about the company's attitude.

hints: Why would it matter that only one thing changed?

strategy.explanation: Ask what the next paragraph's result needs.

candidates.remember: Holding everything else constant lets one change explain a result.

candidates.stem: According to Passage A, the choice of a default is "never neutral" because:

choices.A: employers choose defaults that benefit themselves more than workers.
choices.B: most people take no action, so the default decides what happens to them.
choices.C: a default forbids people from making a different choice.
choices.D: people who opt out of a default must pay a fee to do so.

candidates.evidence: Because doing nothing is what most people do most of the time
candidates.explanation: Since most people do nothing, whatever the default is becomes their outcome; no choice of default leaves outcomes unaffected.

A.rationale: Passage A never questions employers' motives.

C.rationale: Passage A says a default 'does not forbid anything.'

D.rationale: Passage A says a default does not 'cost anyone money.'

hints: What do most people do most of the time?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence that begins with 'Because.'

candidates.remember: A 'because' clause right before a claim usually gives its reason.

candidates.subskill: Meaning of a word in context
candidates.stem: As it is used in the last paragraph of Passage A, the word "exercised" most nearly means:
candidates.evidence: freedom is exercised by busy, distracted human beings
candidates.explanation: To exercise a freedom or right is to use it; the sentence says busy, distracted people are the ones using their freedom.

A.rationale: This is a familiar meaning of 'exercise,' but freedom is not being trained here.

B.rationale: Exercise can strengthen a muscle, but the sentence is about who uses freedom, not about making it stronger.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests freedom is being questioned.

strategy.explanation: Replace the word with your own.

candidates.remember: Test familiar meanings against the sentence before choosing one.

candidates.stem: In Passage B, the statement that the default "held them in place" refers to:

choices.A: a rule requiring enrolled workers to remain in the plan.
choices.B: the employer's refusal to offer any other investment choices.
choices.C: the low rate at which enrolled workers left their jobs early.
choices.D: workers' tendency to keep the default rate and investment.

candidates.evidence: Most automatically enrolled workers stayed at the plan's default contribution rate
candidates.explanation: The preceding sentences say most enrolled workers kept the default rate and default fund; 'held them in place' describes that inertia, not any rule.

A.rationale: Passage A says workers kept their freedom to leave; nothing required them to stay.

B.rationale: Passage A says the investment choices did not change.

hints: What did most enrolled workers do after joining?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentences before the phrase.

candidates.remember: Figurative phrases usually sum up the sentences around them.

candidates.stem: The second paragraph of Passage B mainly serves to:

choices.A: argue that the drawback comes from the same tendency that makes defaults work.
choices.B: concede that the drawback in the first paragraph is too rare to matter much.
choices.C: explain why employers usually choose such low default contribution rates.
choices.D: reject the claim that automatic enrollment actually increases participation.

candidates.evidence: This is not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself, seen from the other side.
candidates.explanation: The paragraph links the drawback (people stay at a low default) to the mechanism behind defaults' success (people stay with whatever requires no action): the same inertia cuts both ways.

B.rationale: The paragraph says the effects can last 'for decades' in 'millions of accounts.'

C.rationale: Employers' reasons for choosing rates are never discussed.

D.rationale: Passage B begins by saying no one disputes that it does.

hints: What tendency makes a default work?
candidates.remember: A paragraph that reframes a problem often links it to an earlier strength.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must recognize the 'two sides of one tendency' argument; the 'too rare to matter' choice misreads the paragraph's tone.

candidates.stem: Passage B suggests that the program in which contribution rates rose with each raise succeeded largely because it:

choices.A: required employees to save a larger share of the pay they already had.
choices.B: offered higher employer matching contributions to those who joined.
choices.C: relied on the inertia that also makes a poor default hard to escape.
choices.D: prevented employees from lowering their contribution rates later.

candidates.evidence: few later bothered to stop them
candidates.explanation: Few people 'bothered to stop' the increases: the program used the same inertia that, according to paragraph 2, keeps people at a poor default, this time to raise savings.

A.rationale: The increases came from future pay, not current pay.

B.rationale: No matching contributions are mentioned for this program.

D.rationale: Few 'bothered to stop' the increases, which implies they could have.

hints: Why did the increases keep happening?
candidates.remember: A program 'putting a tendency to better use' still depends on that tendency.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must connect 'few bothered to stop them' to paragraph 2's inertia; the 'prevented employees from lowering' choice tempts quick readers.

candidates.subskill: Point of agreement between paired passages
candidates.stem: Based on the passages, both authors would most likely agree that:

choices.A: automatic enrollment leads most workers to save more money overall.
choices.B: a default matters greatly because many people never change it.
choices.C: employers should be required by law to enroll workers automatically.
choices.D: the default contribution rates in most plans are set too high.

candidates.explanation: Passage A says the choice of a default is 'never neutral' because most people do nothing; Passage B says 'the default is the policy' because it decides for everyone who never decides.

A.rationale: Passage B says some enrolled workers ended up saving less.

D.rationale: Passage B says the default rate was often low, not high.

hints: What does each passage say about who chooses the default?

strategy.explanation: Test each choice against both passages.

candidates.remember: An agreement answer must be supported by both passages, not just one.

candidates.stem: Passage B's discussion of contribution rates most directly complicates the impression, given in Passage A, that:

choices.A: participation in the plan rose sharply after the rule changed.
choices.B: the rise in participation was largest among younger, lower-income workers.
choices.C: a default respects people's freedom to make a different choice.
choices.D: the jump in participation meant that enrolled workers were saving more.

candidates.evidence: Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less.
candidates.explanation: Passage A presents the participation jump as a success; Passage B shows that participation and saving are different, since many enrolled workers stayed at a low rate and some saved less than they otherwise would have.

A.rationale: Passage B accepts this: 'No one disputes' that automatic enrollment raises participation.

B.rationale: Passage B does not address which groups gained most.

C.rationale: Passage B does not challenge the freedom to opt out.

hints: What does Passage B accept, and what does it question?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate claims Passage B accepts or ignores.

candidates.remember: To 'complicate' a claim, a passage must address it, not merely change the subject.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must separate what Passage B accepts (participation) from what it questions (amount saved); the participation choice is a strong trap.

candidates.subskill: Applying one passage to the other
candidates.stem: Based on Passage B, which workers in the study described in Passage A were most likely made worse off by automatic enrollment?

choices.A: Workers who opted out of the plan as soon as they were enrolled
choices.B: Younger workers who would not have joined the plan under the old rule
choices.C: Workers who would have joined anyway and chosen a higher rate
choices.D: Workers who would have chosen the default investment on their own

candidates.evidence: Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less.
candidates.explanation: Passage B identifies those harmed as workers who would have enrolled anyway at a higher rate but stayed at the low default. Passage A's biggest gainers, younger workers, are the opposite group.

A.rationale: Opting out returns them to their old position; Passage B does not say they were harmed.

B.rationale: These workers gained the most according to Passage A.

D.rationale: Getting the investment they would have chosen leaves them no worse off.

hints: Which workers does Passage B say ended up saving less?

strategy.explanation: Match Passage B's description to a group from Passage A's study.

candidates.remember: Apply one passage's claim to the specific people described in the other.

author_checklist.hardness: Students must map Passage B's general claim onto Passage A's study; the 'younger workers' choice reverses Passage A's finding.
